title: How Long Should You Wait for a Crown After a Root Canal?
metaTitle: How Long to Wait for a Crown After Root Canal
metaDescription: How soon you should get a crown after a root canal, why waiting too long raises fracture and reinfection risk, and the factors that affect timing.
secondaryKeywords: how long to wait for crown after root canal
when to get crown after root canal
excerpt: Why the crown after a root canal should not be put off too long, and what influences the right timing for your tooth.
heroImageAlt: A dental calendar and model tooth suggesting scheduling a crown appointment after a root canal.
bodyHtml:
In general, a crown should be placed within a few weeks of a root canal rather than months later, because a tooth waiting with only a temporary filling is more exposed to fracture and to bacteria leaking back in. There is no single deadline that fits every tooth, and your dentist will give you a specific recommendation, but the guiding principle is clear: do not leave the permanent restoration for too long. Timely restoration is one of the factors that supports a durable outcome.

Why waiting too long is a problem

A tooth that has had a root canal is often already weakened and has had more structure removed to clean the canals. Until it is covered by a crown, it relies on a temporary filling, which is only a short-term seal. Two risks grow the longer that situation continues:

  • Fracture: an unprotected back tooth absorbing full chewing forces can crack, and some fractures cannot be repaired, which may lead to losing the tooth.
  • Reinfection: temporary materials can wear or leak over time, letting bacteria re-enter the cleaned canals and potentially undermining the root canal that was just completed.

Placing the crown within the recommended window reduces both risks.

So what is the right timing?

Many dentists aim to restore the tooth within a few weeks once it is comfortable and the treatment is confirmed to be settling well. Sometimes a brief wait makes sense, for example to allow symptoms to calm or to confirm healing, and sometimes the restoration can proceed quite promptly. The point is that any delay should be intentional and guided by your dentist, not simply the result of putting the appointment off. If life gets busy and the crown keeps getting postponed, it is worth prioritising.

Factors that influence timing

  • Which tooth it is, since high-force molars are a greater fracture concern
  • How much natural tooth structure remains
  • Whether the tooth still has symptoms the dentist wants to see settle
  • Whether a post or additional build-up is needed before the crown
  • Your overall dental treatment plan and scheduling

Because these vary, two people can be given different timelines and both can be appropriate.

While you wait

During the interval before your crown, protect the tooth: chew on the other side, avoid hard and sticky foods, keep up gentle brushing and flossing, and look after the temporary filling. If the temporary comes out or the tooth starts to hurt, contact your dentist rather than continuing to wait, since the tooth may be unsealed. It also helps to book the crown appointment before you leave the office rather than planning to call later, so the timing does not quietly slip. If scheduling is a challenge, let your dental team know, as they can often help you find a workable date within the recommended window.

What if I already waited several months?

If significant time has passed, see your dentist for an assessment rather than assuming all is well. They can check whether the tooth is intact and whether the root canal remains sound, and advise on the best way forward. Acting sooner is better than waiting longer.

Can the tooth be crowned the same day as the root canal?

Sometimes the sequence allows earlier restoration, and in other cases a short interval is preferred. The approach depends on the tooth and the dentist's method, so ask what is planned for your situation.

Does a temporary filling ever last long enough on its own?

Temporary fillings are designed for the short term and are not a permanent solution. They can wear, chip, or leak with time, and relying on one indefinitely leaves the tooth at ongoing risk, which is why the crown or final restoration matters so much to the outcome.

Planning your crown

If you have had a root canal and need to arrange the crown, booking it within the recommended timeframe protects your tooth.
